doc.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Guys and Dolls
summary: He plays the original Guys and Dolls for three years, with a closing night as funny as opening night.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: He allowed me to go. Then shortly thereafter – I went back to the Diamond Horseshoe, and shortly after that I got a call to do another show. Of course I went to him and said, “I got a call to do another show,” and he said, “Young man, I think maybe you should do it, but if it goes beyond four weeks,” he said, “this time I have to get somebody else to take your place.” I thanked him. He said, “Okay, I’ll let you go.” And I went. The show was Guys and Dolls, and it ran for three years.
Whoa. So you were in the first . . . .
The original Guys and Dolls, with Robert Alda, Vivian Blaine, Tom Petty, B. S. Pulley, Stubby Kaye. I can’t remember all the others, but those were some of the principals. It was a good show.
Were you involved in it as it was working itself up? Were you involved in the tryouts and everything?

No, I didn’t go on the road with it, but we did the tryouts here in New York. They would always come in, and you’d have three or four weeks, sometimes five weeks of tryouts. But that one was destined to be a hit even from the start. It was funny.
Was there much change from the first rehearsal to the . . . ?

I don’t think very much. Not very much. They would tighten up certain scenes that they thought maybe were too long or not long enough, things like that. And the dialogue of course they would get really tight, so it was one thing went right into the other. They segued very smoothly. It was one of the funniest shows I think I ever saw. And on closing night, after three years – it actually would have gone longer, but I think there was a hassle with the money. The people who were the principals wanted more money, and the people who were producing the show – I think were Feuer and Martin, who – in fact they were the producers of the show. It seems that their approach, their attitude was that the show was so strong, material-wise, that it really didn’t matter that much who the principals were. So why pay people a lot more money, which was

probably miniscule by today’s standards, but they refused to do it. People, they just said okay. They just left. The show began to get weaker, and of course it closed. But it was still funny on closing night. We in the orchestra were laughing as loud on closing night as we did on opening night. It was a good show.
That’s remarkable after three years of watching the same jokes, to still be able to laugh.
Oh yeah. Every night it was – you just enjoyed it. It was such a lively show, so much entertainment.
